title: What Is a Financial Health Score?

data.text: 30-second answer

A financial health score is a compact way to summarise several aspects of a household's financial position into one easier-to-read result. A useful score does not replace the underlying numbers: it should point back to cash flow, liquidity, debt, assets, resilience, goals and other component measures so the user can see what is driving it. It is also different from a credit score. Its purpose is financial-health interpretation and tracking, not predicting whether a lender will approve a loan.
Key takeaways

items: A headline score is a summary layer, not the household's complete financial story.
The score should be traceable to component metrics and their definitions, with versioned methodology and visible data confidence.
A financial health score is not the same as a credit score, investment-return score or wealth ranking.
Trend and component movement can be more useful than reacting to a single point estimate.
Benchmarks can add context, but the comparison group and evidence quality must be disclosed rather than presented as universal truth.

data.text: Why use a score at all?

Household finances contain many numbers: income, surplus, emergency savings, debt payments, net worth, insurance, investment concentration and goal progress. Reading every number separately can make it difficult to answer the first question a user often has: 'How am I doing overall?' A score can provide that starting point.

The benefit comes from compression. Instead of expecting a user to interpret ten or twenty indicators before understanding the broad picture, the score summarises them and then invites a drill-down. The danger is also compression: if the score hides its ingredients, it can create false confidence.
A good score has a transparent path back to the data

The user should be able to move from the headline score to pillars or components, then to the underlying metric and source data. If debt pressure weakened the score, the system should show which debt measure contributed. If missing data reduced confidence, that should be visible rather than silently filled with a flattering assumption.

For FHIP, score calculation belongs in deterministic, version-controlled logic. Resource content can explain what the result means, but it should not invent a formula or weight that is not in the approved product methodology.
It is not a credit score

A credit score is generally designed for credit-risk or lending contexts and is based on a specific credit-data framework. A financial health score has a different purpose: it is intended to help the household understand the strength and balance of its own financial position.

Someone can have a strong credit history while still having weak emergency liquidity or poor goal readiness. Another person can be debt-free but have low income stability. Treating a financial-health score as a lending score would therefore confuse two different questions.
Worked example: same income, different financial health

Imagine two households each receive 8,000 of monthly take-home income. Household A saves 1,200 a month, keeps four months of essential expenses in accessible cash and has manageable debt payments. Household B spends nearly all of its income, has less than one month of accessible reserves and has rising high-cost debt. Income alone cannot distinguish the two positions.

A multi-component financial health score could summarise the difference, but the most useful output would still show the component pattern: A's stronger liquidity and cash flow versus B's immediate debt and resilience pressure. The exact FHIP scoring weights are governed by the approved methodology, not by this educational example.
Scores need data confidence

A precise number based on incomplete data can be less trustworthy than a preliminary score with a clear warning. If liabilities are missing, net worth and debt metrics can be overstated. If expenses are incomplete, cash-flow and resilience measures may look stronger than they are.
FHIP should therefore distinguish score result from data confidence or completeness. Users should be encouraged to correct missing or stale inputs before treating small score movements as meaningful.
Scores are most useful as a conversation starter

A headline number can help a household prioritise where to look next: cash flow, resilience, debt, goals or another pillar. It can also provide a consistent way to track progress after the underlying data is updated.

It should not be read as a judgement of personal success. Financial circumstances differ by age, household structure, country, income, responsibilities and life stage. The score is a measurement tool for an agreed framework, not a universal label of a person.
Where benchmarks fit

Peer or planning benchmarks can make a metric easier to interpret, but every comparison needs context. A savings rate for a young renter, a family with childcare costs and a retiree does not carry the same meaning. Population data may also be unavailable or not directly comparable across countries.

FHIP's benchmark layer should identify whether a comparison is an observed peer benchmark, an indicative planning range or another reference class. Unsupported percentile claims should not be fabricated.
How to read the FHIP score responsibly

Start with the headline result, then inspect the weakest and strongest components, data confidence, recent movement and any explanation of what changed. If one component is driving most of the result, review that underlying module rather than trying to 'improve the score' as an end in itself.
The goal is better financial health and clearer decisions. A higher number only matters if it reflects genuine improvement in the underlying household position.
Frequently asked questions
Is a financial health score the same as my credit score?

No. A credit score serves a credit-risk purpose. A financial health score summarises a broader household financial-health framework and should not be used as a substitute for a lender's credit assessment.
What is a good FHIP score?

The meaning of any band must come from the approved FHIP methodology shown in the product. This article does not invent a universal cut-off. Components and data confidence should always be read with the headline result.
Can two people have the same score for different reasons?
Yes. One person may have strong liquidity and weaker goal progress while another has the opposite pattern. That is why component drill-down matters.
Should I compare my score with other people?
A comparison can add context if the cohort and data source are appropriate. It should not be treated as a judgement or as proof that your own goals are suitable.
How often should the score change?
It should change when relevant underlying data or approved methodology changes. Small movements should be interpreted cautiously, especially when data is incomplete or volatile values have moved.

title: Why One Score Cannot Describe Your Entire Financial Position

data.text: 30-second answer

One score cannot describe an entire financial position because different households can reach the same headline result through very different combinations of cash flow, debt, liquidity, assets, resilience and future readiness. The score is useful as an entry point, but the component pattern tells you what the number actually means. A responsible financial-health system therefore shows the score, the drivers behind it, the quality of the data and the direction of change.
Key takeaways

items: The same headline score can hide opposite strengths and weaknesses.
Components, data completeness and trend should be reviewed before acting on a score.
A higher net worth or income does not automatically produce strong liquidity, manageable debt or goal readiness.
A score should prioritise investigation, not become a target to game by changing one metric without improving the household position.
FHIP explanations should trace every major score movement back to deterministic inputs and rules.

data.text: A score compresses information - and compression loses detail

Any score turns many measurements into a smaller number of outputs. That makes a dashboard easier to scan, but it also means information is being compressed. Two households can therefore land in the same broad band while facing different financial decisions.
This is normal, not a flaw, provided the platform keeps the drill-down available. The problem starts when the headline number is treated as a complete diagnosis.
Worked example: two households, one headline result

Consider an illustrative framework with several components but no claim about FHIP's actual weights. Household A has a stable monthly surplus and six months of emergency liquidity, but carries a high debt-service burden and has weak retirement progress. Household B has little debt and strong long-term assets, but only one month of accessible cash and a volatile monthly surplus.

A scoring model could plausibly place both households near the same overall level even though the next useful review is different. A should investigate debt pressure and future funding; B should investigate liquidity and cash-flow stability. The headline number alone cannot tell that story.
Look for the shape of the score

The 'shape' means the pattern of component results. Which pillars are strong? Which are weak? Is one severe issue being averaged with several strong areas? Are all components middling? Is the score based on complete data or on only part of the household record?
A component chart can reveal this shape immediately. It also prevents a strong asset position from masking a short-term resilience problem or a strong income from masking debt pressure.
Trend adds another dimension

A score of 65 that has risen steadily from 55 can tell a different story from a score of 65 that has fallen from 78. The current number is identical; the direction is not. Trend should be interpreted alongside changes in the underlying data rather than used as a performance guarantee.

Large jumps also deserve scrutiny. They may reflect a real event such as debt repayment, but they may also come from newly added assets, corrected records, changed valuations or a methodology version. The explanation should distinguish those causes.
Data completeness can be more important than precision

If income and investments are recorded but liabilities are missing, a score can look deceptively strong. If essential expenses are understated, resilience can be overstated. The platform should not reward missing data by treating unknown values as zero where that would materially bias the result.

FHIP's design includes data confidence and completeness concepts precisely because the user needs to know how much evidence sits behind the score. A preliminary result with a clear missing-data prompt can be more useful than a confident-looking but incomplete score.
Do not optimise the score at the expense of the household

Once a score exists, it can be tempting to focus on the number itself. But financial health is the objective, not the score. Moving money from accessible cash into a volatile investment might improve one theoretical metric while weakening short-term resilience. Paying down debt aggressively might reduce interest but create a cash shortage if the household has no emergency buffer.
A good recommendation system therefore considers trade-offs and dependencies. It should explain the underlying problem and estimated impact rather than simply saying 'do this to gain points'.
Benchmarks do not remove the need for context

A peer comparison can show whether a component is unusual within a defined cohort, but it cannot know every household's priorities. A high-income family with large childcare costs, a recent migrant building a new balance sheet and a pre-retiree can reasonably look different.
The comparison should disclose cohort breadth, data quality and whether the reference is a real observed benchmark or an indicative planning range.
How FHIP should present a score

The most useful sequence is: headline score, confidence, component breakdown, plain-English driver explanation, relevant comparison where available, and a link to the module where the underlying data can be reviewed. This keeps the score explainable and action-oriented.
If the user asks 'Why is my score this number?', the answer should be traceable to actual recorded values and approved rules - not an invented AI explanation.
Frequently asked questions
If my overall score is strong, can I ignore weak components?
No. A material weakness can still matter even when other components lift the average. Review the component and its real-world consequence.
Why can my score move after I correct data?

Because the score uses the recorded inputs. Adding a missing debt, changing an outdated asset value or correcting expenses can change the result even though the household itself did not change that day.
Should every component have the same weight?
Not necessarily. Weighting is a methodology decision. For FHIP, only the approved version-controlled methodology should determine actual weights.
Can a low score mean someone is financially irresponsible?
No. The score describes a modelled financial position, not character, effort or personal worth. Circumstances and data quality matter.
What should I look at first?
Start with any high-risk or materially weak component, then consider data confidence and the household's immediate obligations. The relevant FHIP module should show the underlying evidence.

title: How FHIP Calculates Debt Service Ratio

data.text: 30-second answer

FHIP's current canonical debt-service ratio measures required monthly debt repayments relative to net monthly household income. At a high level: required monthly debt repayments divided by net monthly income, expressed as a percentage. If required repayments are 2,000 and net income is 8,000, DSR is 25%. If net income is zero, FHIP should show Not Available rather than Infinity or NaN.
Key takeaways

items: DSR is a cash-flow pressure measure, not a debt-balance measure.
Current canonical formula: required monthly debt repayments / net monthly income x 100.
Use the same period for repayments and income and include each repayment once.
Zero or invalid net-income denominators must return Not Available.
FHIP DSR and FHIP DTI answer different questions: repayment burden versus balance-sheet leverage.

data.text: What debt service is designed to show

Debt service is the cash a household must use to meet required debt repayments during the period. Comparing that cash requirement with net income shows how much of the household's usable monthly income is already committed before other financial goals are considered.

A household can have a large debt balance but a manageable current repayment if the loan term is long and the rate is low. Another can have a smaller balance but high cash-flow pressure because the term is short, the rate is high or several repayments overlap. DSR focuses on this monthly burden.
High-level FHIP formula
Current working formula: Debt service ratio = Required monthly debt repayments / Net monthly household income x 100.

Repayments must be normalised to a monthly basis and should represent the required payment amounts defined in the liability data model. Net monthly income must come from the same canonical income service used by the current-state cash-flow metrics.
Worked FHIP example

Assume required monthly repayments are 2,000 and net monthly household income is 8,000. DSR = 2,000 / 8,000 x 100 = 25%. This means one quarter of the net income measure is committed to required debt repayments.

If repayments rise to 2,800 while income remains 8,000, DSR rises to 35%. If income falls to 7,000 with repayments still 2,000, DSR becomes about 28.6%. The ratio can therefore worsen because repayments rise, income falls, or both.
Repayment inclusion and double-counting controls

The debt-service numerator should be derived from active included liabilities and current required repayment amounts. Closed or fully repaid debts should not continue to contribute. Duplicate debt records must not be counted twice.

The same repayment can also appear in household cash-flow outflows. That is expected for cash-flow aggregation, but the system must still maintain one canonical repayment amount rather than independently calculating a different number for DSR, Dashboard and Reports.
Why denominator governance matters

Debt ratios are not globally standardised. Some lending or macroeconomic frameworks use gross income, disposable income or other definitions. FHIP's current 50-user canonical evidence uses net monthly income for DSR and the live Score language has described debt repayments as a share of net monthly income.

Older project artifacts may contain a gross-income DSR convention. That historical inconsistency is precisely why this Explainer is product-dependent: before publication, compare the draft with the current production code and active calculation version. If production differs, resolve the methodology rather than publishing two formulas.
Zero income and interpretation limits

When net income is zero, FHIP should show DSR as Not Available. A zero-income household can still face serious repayment pressure, but an infinite percentage is not a useful user-facing metric. The underlying repayment amount and cash-flow deficit should remain visible.
DSR should be read with liquidity, DTI, interest rates, loan maturity, income stability and essential expenses. It does not by itself determine creditworthiness or prescribe a borrowing action.
Frequently asked questions
Is DSR the same as FHIP DTI?
No. FHIP DTI compares debt balances with gross annual income; DSR compares required monthly repayments with net monthly income.
Why does FHIP use net income here?
The current canonical FHIP household metric uses net monthly income to show repayment pressure against usable income. Publication must still be verified against the live calculation service.
What happens if net income is zero?
The ratio should be Not Available, while FHIP continues to show the required repayment amount and other cash-flow evidence.
Do credit-card minimum payments count?
Only according to the approved liability and repayment rules. The production data dictionary must define the required repayment used for each debt type.
Can DSR rise even while debt is falling?
Yes. A rate reset, shorter remaining term or income fall can increase required repayments even as the outstanding balance declines.

How FHIP Measures Emergency Fund Coverage

data.text: 30-second answer

FHIP measures emergency-fund coverage by comparing eligible liquid emergency assets with essential monthly expenses. At a high level: eligible liquid emergency assets divided by essential monthly expenses = months of coverage. If the household has 12,000 of eligible liquid funds and 4,000 of essential monthly expenses, the coverage is 3 months. Total net worth is not used as a substitute for immediately accessible liquidity.
Key takeaways

items: Coverage is measured in months, not only as a cash balance.
Use eligible liquid emergency assets, not every asset the household owns.
Use essential monthly expenses from the same governed expense classification.
Zero, missing or unreliable denominators need safe governed handling rather than Infinity/NaN.
The number is one resilience input; it is not a universal instruction that every household needs the same target.

data.text: What emergency-fund coverage is designed to show

An emergency fund is valuable because it buys time when normal cash flow is disrupted. A dollar balance alone does not tell the household how much time it represents. Coverage converts accessible reserves into months of essential spending so the number has practical meaning.

This is a short-term resilience measure. A household may have high net worth because of property, retirement accounts or long-term investments and still have weak emergency coverage if little of that wealth is available promptly and reliably.
High-level FHIP formula
Current working formula: Emergency-fund coverage (months) = Eligible liquid emergency assets / Essential monthly expenses.

Both parts require governed classifications. Liquid emergency assets should be resources the approved Resilience methodology treats as available for a shock. Essential monthly expenses should represent costs that are expected to continue, using the current expense classifications and frequency-normalised amounts.
Worked FHIP example
Assume eligible liquid emergency assets are 12,000 and essential monthly expenses are 4,000. Coverage = 12,000 / 4,000 = 3 months.

Now assume essential expenses increase to 4,800 while the reserve stays at 12,000. Coverage falls to 2.5 months. Nothing was withdrawn from the emergency fund; the household's required monthly runway simply became more expensive.
What should count as liquid

Liquidity is about access, stability and restrictions. Cash and approved near-cash balances may be eligible. Property, restricted retirement assets and illiquid private investments can contribute to net worth but generally do not perform the same immediate emergency function unless the approved methodology explicitly says otherwise.

Market investments can sometimes be sold, but their value can move and access can involve settlement time, tax or transaction consequences. FHIP should therefore follow the configured eligibility treatment rather than automatically count all investments at full value.
Essential expenses matter as much as the reserve

The denominator determines how long the reserve can last. Essential expenses can include housing, basic food, utilities, necessary transport, required debt repayments and other unavoidable costs according to the product classification. Predictable discretionary spending should not automatically be treated as essential simply because it has historically occurred.
Users should be able to understand the essential-expense figure and correct classifications. Otherwise the months-of-coverage result can look precise while being based on an unrealistic denominator.
Edge cases and data confidence

If essential monthly expenses are zero, missing or incomplete, the calculation must follow the production safe-denominator policy. It should never display Infinity or NaN. A confirmed zero is also different from missing expense data and should carry the correct interpretation.

FHIP should show the coverage alongside data confidence and other resilience drivers such as income concentration, debt commitments and protection. A single months figure does not guarantee that every shock can be funded.
Frequently asked questions
Does FHIP count my home in emergency-fund coverage?
Not merely because it is part of net worth. The emergency metric should use assets that satisfy the approved liquidity eligibility rules.
Why use essential expenses instead of all spending?
A resilience stress test focuses on costs that would continue during a shock. Some discretionary spending may be reducible, but the exact classification must be realistic and governed.
Is three months a FHIP target?
Not automatically. Several months is common educational guidance, but the platform should use only approved reference ranges and explain that household circumstances differ.
What if essential expenses are zero?
The production methodology should return a safe governed result, normally Not Available or an explicitly defined special case, rather than divide by zero.
Can insurance replace an emergency fund?
Insurance and emergency liquidity do different jobs. Policies cover defined events subject to terms, waiting periods and exclusions; cash can cover immediate costs more broadly.

How FHIP Calculates Debt-to-Income Ratio

data.text: 30-second answer

FHIP's balance-based debt-to-income measure compares total included household liabilities with gross annual household income. At a high level: total included liabilities divided by gross annual income, expressed as a multiple. If liabilities are 420,000 and gross annual income is 120,000, FHIP DTI is 3.5x. This definition is different from the monthly debt-payment ratio often called DTI in consumer lending, so FHIP must always show the formula label.
Key takeaways

items: FHIP DTI is a stock-of-debt leverage measure: total included liabilities / gross annual income.
Express the result as a multiple such as 3.5x unless the product UI explicitly formats it another governed way.
Use active canonical liability balances and annualised gross recurring household income.
Do not confuse DTI with FHIP debt-service ratio, which measures required repayments relative to net monthly income.
Zero or missing gross income requires safe N/A treatment rather than division by zero.

data.text: Why FHIP needs a balance-based leverage measure

Two households can have similar monthly repayments but very different amounts of debt outstanding. A balance-based DTI helps show the scale of total liabilities relative to the household's annual earning base. It therefore complements, rather than replaces, the cash-flow view provided by debt service.

This metric is particularly useful when looking at leverage over time: debt can decline as principal is repaid, or rise because new borrowing is added, even before the required monthly repayment changes materially.
High-level FHIP formula
Current working formula: Debt-to-income ratio = Total included liabilities / Gross annual household income.

The result is naturally expressed as a multiple. Gross annual household income should be annualised from the approved recurring gross-income records. Total liabilities should come from active canonical liability balances so the same debt is not counted twice through duplicated records or derived views.
Worked FHIP example
Assume total included liabilities are 420,000. Gross household income is 10,000 per month, or 120,000 per year. DTI = 420,000 / 120,000 = 3.5x.

If the debt balance falls to 360,000 while annual gross income stays at 120,000, DTI falls to 3.0x. If income rises to 140,000 with debt still 420,000, DTI also falls, to 3.0x. The measure changes when either the debt stock or the annual earning base changes.
Why the label can be confusing

In many consumer-lending contexts, debt-to-income is defined as monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income. That is a legitimate but different convention. FHIP's current balance-based metric is closer to a leverage multiple and should be named and explained explicitly so users do not compare unlike percentages or multiples.

The safest presentation is to show the formula or a short methodology link wherever DTI appears. If FHIP later changes the definition, the content, reports, benchmarks and historical calculation version must change together.
What goes into total liabilities and income

Liabilities should follow the canonical active-debt register: for example, included mortgages, personal loans, vehicle finance, credit-card balances and other approved debt categories. Offsets, duplicate records, closed debts and uncertain values require the treatment specified by the data dictionary.

Gross annual income should use approved recurring household income records and the standard frequency conversion. One-off windfalls should not silently become annual recurring income. Cross-border income must be converted consistently into the reporting basis before it is combined, if the metric is shown on a consolidated household basis.
Edge cases and interpretation

If gross annual income is zero or missing, the ratio cannot be interpreted conventionally and should be Not Available under the safe-denominator policy. A high or low DTI is not by itself a credit decision or personal recommendation; debt cost, repayment burden, liquidity, asset backing, income stability and household circumstances still matter.
Frequently asked questions
Why is FHIP DTI a multiple rather than a percentage?
Because the numerator is a debt balance and the denominator is annual income. A 420,000 balance divided by 120,000 of annual income is 3.5 times income.
Is this the same DTI a bank uses for a mortgage application?
Not necessarily. Many lenders use monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income and may apply product-specific rules. Always compare formulas before comparing values.
Does a mortgage count?
If it is an active included household liability under the current FHIP data dictionary, its outstanding balance contributes to total liabilities.
What if income is zero?
FHIP should return Not Available rather than an infinite multiple.
Is lower always better?
Lower leverage generally means less debt relative to income, but the ratio does not describe interest cost, repayment flexibility, asset quality or all household circumstances.

How FHIP Measures Retirement Readiness

data.text: 30-second answer

FHIP retirement readiness is not safely described by one universal percentage. The product can show a current Retirement Readiness component in the Financial Health Score and can also run a longer-term retirement forecast using recorded retirement balances, contributions, retirement timing, spending/target assumptions and other governed inputs. Those views are related but different. The current production score methodology determines the component score; the Forecasting engine estimates future balances, target or required corpus, funding gap and contribution path. Public content must keep the two layers distinct and must not invent a single formula that merges them.
Key takeaways

items: Current Retirement Readiness score and long-term retirement forecast are related but distinct product outputs.
Forecasting can use retirement balances, contribution path, retirement timing, target/desired income and approved inflation/return assumptions.
Australia superannuation and India EPF/PPF/NPS categories are supported in the retirement architecture, subject to the active implementation.
A missing date of birth or retirement timing can limit readiness interpretation even when FHIP can still show an accumulation trajectory.
Retirement projections are scenarios under assumptions, not guarantees, and both nominal and inflation-adjusted views may be relevant.

data.text: Two layers of retirement readiness inside FHIP

The Financial Health Score can include a Retirement Readiness component that summarises the household’s current retirement position according to the active score methodology. Current report evidence has described this component using a rough age-based reference comparison. That is useful as a current-state indicator but should not be confused with a full retirement plan.

The Forecasting module answers a different question: based on recorded balances, contributions, time to retirement and approved assumptions, what could the retirement position look like in the future, and how does that compare with the user’s target or required retirement resources?
High-level retirement-forecast flow

At a high level: validate retirement timing -> collect current retirement balances by account/category -> include eligible future contributions -> apply approved return and inflation assumptions -> project retirement resources through time -> compare projected resources with the target/required corpus or income goal -> show gap and contribution sensitivity.

The current implementation must determine which balances and contribution types are eligible. Australia superannuation and India EPF, PPF and NPS need correct country/currency treatment and should not be duplicated in both general assets and retirement totals.
Worked interpretation example

A real FHIP report example has shown a Retirement Readiness component of 43/100 together with wording that the recorded retirement balance was about 36% of a rough age-based guideline. That is current-state score evidence from that specific report version; it is not a universal retirement formula.

A full retirement forecast can then show a projected balance at retirement, an estimated required retirement corpus under the chosen method, and the remaining funding gap. If the projected resources are 900,000 and the approved target is 1,200,000, the illustrative gap is 300,000. The actual FHIP result must come from the live forecast run and assumptions rather than this example.
Why retirement timing matters

Years to retirement affect compounding, contributions and the period over which the household needs to build resources. Date of birth and intended retirement age/date therefore materially improve the analysis.

If date of birth is missing but another valid timing input exists, the production engine may still be able to estimate years to retirement. If timing is insufficient, FHIP can show an accumulation trajectory but should explain that a reliable retirement-age readiness assessment is not yet available.
Targets, inflation and purchasing power

Retirement goals can be framed as a target balance, desired retirement income/spending, or another approved method. Each method has different assumptions. FHIP should identify which method produced the target and preserve the assumption set with the forecast.

Long-term nominal figures can look large simply because prices and incomes change over time. Where the active product supports it, nominal and inflation-adjusted results should both be available so users can separate future-dollar growth from purchasing-power interpretation.
Scenario sensitivity and limitations

Retirement outcomes are sensitive to returns, inflation, contribution behaviour, fees, retirement timing, longevity, tax and policy rules. FHIP should therefore present scenarios and sensitivities as educational modelling rather than predictions.

A user can explore what changes if retirement is earlier, contributions are different or returns/inflation move within approved scenarios. The platform must not present an optimistic case as the expected case or recommend a specific investment or retirement product.
Frequently asked questions
Is my Retirement Readiness score the same as my projected retirement gap?
No. The score is a current product component under the score methodology; the forecast gap is a future projection against a target/required corpus.
Why does FHIP need my date of birth or retirement age?
Timing determines how long contributions and compounding can continue and when the retirement target is assessed.
Can FHIP forecast retirement if some timing information is missing?
It may still show an accumulation path if sufficient inputs exist, but it should clearly state when retirement-age readiness cannot be calculated reliably.
Does reaching a target guarantee I will have enough?
No. Targets and projections depend on assumptions and future circumstances. FHIP is an educational planning tool, not a guarantee.
Does the forecast include super, EPF, PPF and NPS?
The approved architecture supports these categories, but the exact included records and treatment must match the current production implementation and jurisdiction rules.

title: What Is Financial Health? | GKTC x FHIP

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Explain financial health as the ability to manage today, absorb shocks, make progress toward goals and retain flexibility. Show why salary or wealth alone is not enough, then connect the idea to the FHIP Dashboard and Financial Health Score.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook

If I told you two people both earn 150,000 a year, could you tell me which one is financially healthier? Probably not. One might have strong savings, low debt and a six-month emergency buffer. The other might spend almost everything, carry heavy repayments and have no accessible reserve.
[VISUAL] Split screen: two households, same income, very different cash flow, debt and emergency reserve.
Financial health is wider than wealth
Financial health is not simply how much you earn or how much you own. It is the overall ability of your household finances to work today and remain useful when life changes.

A financially healthy household can usually meet current commitments, keep some room between income and spending, absorb a reasonable shock, manage debt, build longer-term assets and continue moving toward important goals. No single number can describe all of that.
A simple four-part way to think about it

First, cash flow: is money coming in enough to cover the money that needs to go out? Second, resilience: if income stops or a major expense appears, how much accessible buffer is available? Third, balance sheet and debt: what do you own, what do you owe, and how demanding are the repayments? Fourth, progress: are savings, investments, retirement and goals moving in a sustainable direction?
[VISUAL] Four tiles: Manage Today | Absorb a Shock | Build Strength | Make Progress.
Worked household example

Imagine Household A earns 10,000 a month after tax and spends 9,700. It has a high-value home, but very little cash and large loan repayments. Household B earns 7,000, spends 5,500, has four months of emergency savings and steadily contributes to retirement and other goals.

Household A may look wealthier on paper, but Household B may have stronger day-to-day flexibility and resilience. The point is not that one number proves who is better. The point is that financial health is multidimensional.
The common misunderstanding

A common mistake is to treat a high salary, rising investment portfolio or positive net worth as proof that everything is fine. Each can be a strength, but each can coexist with weak liquidity, unsustainable spending, concentrated debt or inadequate protection.
The reverse is also true. A household with modest income may be financially organised, resilient and steadily improving.
How FHIP connects the picture

FHIP is designed to bring those dimensions together. The Dashboard shows the current financial picture, the Financial Health Score summarises multiple components, and deeper modules let you inspect cash flow, debt, resilience, investments, retirement and goals.
The score is a starting point, not the answer. The useful question is: what is driving my financial position, what has changed, and which area should I understand next?
Recap and CTA
So remember: financial health is the ability to manage today, absorb shocks and keep making progress - not just the amount of money you earn.
If you want to see how your own financial picture fits together, use FHIP to check your financial health. And if this explanation was useful, follow @GKTC for more plain-English financial education.

title: Financial Resilience: Can Your Finances Absorb a Shock?

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Explain financial resilience as the ability to absorb and recover from shocks using liquidity, income stability, debt/fixed commitments, protection and stress capacity. Do not invent FHIP resilience weights.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook

A household can look financially strong on a normal day and still struggle when something unexpected happens. Financial resilience asks a different question: how well can your finances absorb a shock and keep functioning?
[VISUAL] Normal month -> shock -> recovery path.
Resilience is not one bank balance

Cash matters, but resilience is wider than cash. It includes accessible emergency funds, essential spending, stability and concentration of income, debt repayments, fixed commitments, insurance/protection information and the size and duration of the shock being tested.
A simple shock example
Imagine a household with 12,000 of liquid emergency funds and essential expenses of 4,000 a month. That is three months of basic expense coverage before considering any income that continues.

Now imagine income falls by 50% for three months. The actual cash drawdown depends on the remaining income and the household’s fixed commitments. The same three-month reserve can feel very different for two households.
Four questions to ask

One: how much usable liquidity is available? Two: how stable and diversified are income sources? Three: how much spending and debt service cannot easily be reduced? Four: what protection or other resources could help if a specified event occurs?
[VISUAL] Liquidity | Income | Commitments | Protection.
Why asset-rich can still mean fragile

A household may own property and investments but have little cash. Selling an asset can take time, create costs or happen during a weak market. That is why net worth and resilience are not interchangeable.
How FHIP measures resilience

FHIP’s Resilience engine is a governed composite assessment. It brings together approved components and stress conditions and produces an overall result with component risks. The exact weights and thresholds are product methodology and should not be guessed from a public video.
Use resilience to plan, not to predict

A stress test is not a forecast that something bad will happen. It is a way to ask, “If this happened, what would break first, how long could we continue, and what information or buffer would improve the picture?”
FHIP connection and CTA
Use FHIP to check your financial resilience and see the drivers behind the result. And follow @GKTC for more practical financial education.

data.text: Approved plain-English definition
A liability is a financial obligation or amount owed by a person or household.
What it means

Common liabilities include mortgages, personal loans, vehicle loans and credit-card balances. The outstanding balance affects the balance sheet, while the required repayment affects cash flow. Those are related but different measures.
Mini example
If a household has a 350,000 mortgage and a 5,000 credit-card balance, its included liabilities total 355,000 before considering any methodology-specific exclusions.

title: How to Read Your FHIP Free Report

data.text: 30-second answer

Read the FHIP Free Report as a guided explanation of one canonical household financial snapshot, not as a separate calculator. Start with the report identity, reporting period/currency and data confidence; then read the Financial Health Score and plain-English summary; review cash flow, assets, liabilities, net worth, emergency liquidity and debt; inspect the component/pillar evidence and goals/actions; and finish with data-quality notes, methodology/version information and the disclaimer. The exact page count and layout can evolve, so this Resource must be checked against the active Free Report template immediately before publication.
Key takeaways

items: First confirm the report month, snapshot date, reporting currency, report version/status and data confidence.
The headline score is a summary; use the underlying cash-flow, balance-sheet, resilience and component evidence to understand it.
All numbers should reconcile to the same canonical snapshot used by the Dashboard and other modules; the report should not invent independent totals.
Missing or insufficient data should produce useful fallback messages explaining what is needed rather than blank charts or guessed values.
The report is educational information, not personal financial, investment, tax, legal or credit advice.

data.text: 1 - begin with the report identity and scope

The first page tells you whose household the report covers, the reporting month, the financial-position snapshot date and the reporting currency. These details matter because a balance-sheet number is only meaningful for a particular date and currency.

Also note the report ID/version/status and data-confidence message where shown. If two reports were generated from different snapshots or methodology versions, their numbers may legitimately differ. FHIP should make the source snapshot and version traceable.
2 - read the headline score and plain-English position

The score section gives a fast summary of overall financial health under the active model. Read the headline together with the band, data confidence and the short explanation of the household’s current position.

Then look at strengths and areas requiring review. These should come from validated structured facts and approved content libraries, not from a second ungoverned calculation. A “strength” such as positive net worth does not automatically mean liquidity is strong, and an “area to review” is not a personalised product recommendation.
3 - understand money in, money out and surplus

The cash-flow section explains income and recorded outflows for the period, including the distinction between gross and net income and the treatment of essential/discretionary expenses, debt repayments and other commitments. The monthly surplus or deficit shows what remains after the included outflows.

Read the savings rate beside the dollar surplus. A percentage provides scale, while the dollar amount shows the actual capacity. If a number looks inconsistent with the Dashboard, that is a reconciliation issue to investigate rather than something the report should explain away.
4 - review the balance sheet, liquidity and debt

The report brings together assets, liabilities and net worth, then separately looks at accessible emergency resources and debt pressure. These measures answer different questions. Net worth can be positive while liquidity is weak; a household can have manageable total debt but high monthly repayment pressure.

Cross-border holdings must be converted once into the report currency using the approved convention while retaining original-currency evidence. The same investment, retirement account or goal-linked asset should not be counted twice in net worth.
5 - use component evidence and goals to find the next area to understand

A useful Free Report should show the Financial Health Score components or pillars with plain-English meaning, status and a driver or review prompt. The reader should be able to move from the headline score to the underlying reason.

Goal sections should show current progress and, where the Free tier includes it, a broad deterministic readiness/fallback without exposing paid scenario depth. A recommended Free Report design keeps conservative/base/optimistic goal scenario tables out of the Free tier and uses a contextual paid-feature teaser only when a valid paid forecast exists.
6 - finish with data quality, methodology and disclaimer

Before relying on any conclusion, review what information is missing, stale or incomplete. FHIP should distinguish a confirmed zero from missing data and show when a result is not available because the required inputs are absent.

The methodology/version section exists so the report can be reproduced. The disclaimer explains the advice boundary. The Free Report is intended to improve understanding and help users decide what to review next; it does not replace appropriately qualified advice where personal recommendations are required.
Worked reading example

A current FHIP report example begins with a household/report identity page, then shows a Financial Health Score of 82/100 with a band and 90% data confidence. The following pages explain current cash flow, net worth, emergency-fund months, strengths/areas to review and core figures.

The correct reading order is not “82 means everything is fine.” It is: confirm the snapshot/confidence, read 82 as the headline model result, then inspect the cash-flow and balance-sheet evidence, identify the component or goal that needs review, and check the data-quality/methodology notes before drawing conclusions.
Frequently asked questions
Why might my report not match an older report?
The source snapshot, household data, FX rates, assumptions or calculation version may have changed. The report should identify the relevant version and date.
Why is a chart sometimes replaced by a message?
If reliable data is unavailable, FHIP should use a useful fallback explaining what is missing rather than display a blank or misleading visual.
Is the Free Report the same as the Dashboard?
They should use the same canonical facts, but present them differently. The report adds structured explanation and a downloadable review format.
Why does the Free Report not show every forecast scenario?
The Free tier is intentionally focused. Detailed scenarios, diagnostics and other premium depth can be reserved for the paid experience, subject to the active commercial/report design.
Can I use the report as personal financial advice?
No. It is general financial information and education based on data and governed calculations. Personal advice requires the appropriate professional/regulatory context.
CTA: Open My Report

title: How Much Emergency Fund Do You Really Need?

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Explain emergency funds in months of essential expenses, avoid presenting one universal target, show factors that can change the appropriate buffer, and connect to FHIP emergency-fund coverage and Resilience.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook
Is three months enough? Six months? Twelve months? The better question is: enough for what kind of household, with what risks and what access to cash?
[VISUAL] 3 / 6 / 12 months shown as question marks, not targets.
Start with the job of an emergency fund
An emergency fund is readily accessible money reserved for unexpected financial shocks: an income interruption, urgent repair, medical cost or another necessary expense that cannot easily wait.
Its first job is not to earn the highest return. Its first job is to be available when the shock arrives.
Measure the buffer in months

A useful way to understand the reserve is to compare eligible liquid emergency assets with essential monthly expenses. If you have 12,000 available and essential expenses are 4,000 a month, that is three months of coverage.
[VISUAL] 12,000 / 4,000 = 3 months.
Why there is no single perfect number

The appropriate buffer depends on income stability, number of earners, job security, health, dependants, debt repayments, access to insurance, irregular commitments and how quickly the household could reduce spending.

A household with two stable incomes and flexible expenses may view the risk differently from a single-income household with high fixed commitments. General rules of thumb are references, not personal prescriptions.
Emergency savings are not the same as investments

A large investment portfolio does not automatically replace emergency liquidity. Investments can fluctuate, take time to sell or create tax and transaction consequences. An emergency reserve is about reliable access and stability.
Stress-test the household

Instead of arguing over a magic month number, try a simple stress test. What happens if income falls by half for three months? What if a major expense arrives at the same time? Which bills are essential, which can be reduced, and how quickly would the liquid reserve run down?
That exercise makes the emergency-fund question specific to the household without pretending that the future is predictable.
FHIP connection and CTA

FHIP measures emergency-fund coverage and combines liquidity with income, debt, commitments and other factors inside its Resilience view. The purpose is to show how well the household may be able to absorb a shock - not to tell everyone to hold the same cash balance.
Use FHIP to check your financial resilience, and follow @GKTC for more financial education.

title: Compounding Explained Visually

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Explain compounding visually: future growth can occur on original capital plus earlier gains. Use simple math and show why time and return assumptions matter. Do not imply guaranteed investment returns.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook
Compounding is often described as “earning returns on your returns.” That is true, but the easiest way to understand it is to watch the base you are growing from get larger over time.
[VISUAL] 100 growing to 105, then 110.25.
The simplest example

Start with 100. If it grows by 5% in year one, you finish with 105. If the next year also happens to be 5%, the 5% is applied to 105, not the original 100. You finish with 110.25. The extra 0.25 is growth on the previous gain.
After ten years at a purely hypothetical steady 5%, 100 would become about 162.89. That does not mean markets deliver 5% every year. It simply shows the mathematics.
Time changes the effect

Compounding is slow at first because the base is small. Over longer periods, earlier contributions and gains have more time to participate in later returns. That is why time horizon is a major input in investment and retirement forecasts.
Contributions add another layer
If you add money regularly, each contribution begins its own compounding path from the date it is invested. An amount contributed today has more time than the same amount contributed ten years later.
[VISUAL] Timeline with monthly contributions, each growing from a different start point.
Compounding also works against you
Debt interest can compound too. If unpaid interest is added to a balance, future interest may be charged on the larger amount. So compounding is a mechanism, not automatically a benefit.
Real investing is not a smooth line

Actual investment returns vary. Some years can be positive and others negative. Fees, taxes, cash flows and timing affect the result. A forecast that uses a long-term return assumption is a scenario, not a promise that every year will follow that percentage.
FHIP connection and CTA
FHIP uses transparent assumptions when it forecasts investments, goals and retirement. Review the assumptions, time horizon and contribution path rather than focusing only on the final number.
Use FHIP to review your investments and follow @GKTC for more visual finance explanations.

title: Cash Flow

data.text: Approved plain-English definition
Cash flow is money coming into and leaving a household over a period.
What it means

Cash inflows can include salary or other included income. Outflows can include living expenses, debt repayments and other commitments under the relevant calculation. Cash flow is a period measure; it is different from net worth, which is a balance-sheet snapshot at a point in time.
Mini example
If 8,000 comes in during a month and 6,200 of included outflows leave, the month has positive cash flow and a 1,800 surplus.
Related terms
Net Income, Cash Flow Surplus, Cash Flow Deficit
FHIP contextual use

Use Cash Flow to describe money moving into and out of the household over a defined period. FHIP cash-flow analysis should use consistent periods and avoid confusing bank-account balances with income/outflow flows.

Liquidity

data.text: Approved plain-English definition
Liquidity describes how easily an asset can be converted into usable cash.
What it means

Cash in a transaction or savings account is usually highly liquid. Property, a private business interest or some long-term investments may take more time, involve costs or fluctuate in value before they can be turned into cash. High net worth therefore does not automatically mean high liquidity.
Mini example
A household may own a property worth 800,000 but have only 5,000 of readily available cash. Its net worth may be strong while its short-term liquidity is limited.
Related terms
Asset, Emergency Fund, Net Worth
FHIP contextual use
Use Liquidity to explain how quickly and reliably an asset can become usable cash. FHIP should keep liquidity separate from total asset value and net worth when assessing emergency readiness.

title: 7 Numbers Every Household Should Know

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Walk through seven useful household numbers in plain English: net income, monthly expenses/outflows, cash-flow surplus, savings rate, emergency-fund months, debt/repayment pressure and net worth. Explain that each number answers a different question.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook

You do not need 50 financial ratios to understand your household. Start with seven numbers. If you know these seven and update them regularly, you can answer most of the basic questions about where your money is going and how much flexibility you have.
[VISUAL] Large “7” surrounded by seven labelled icons.
1 - Net monthly income

This is the income actually available to run the household after compulsory deductions under the way you are measuring cash flow. It is different from gross salary. Net income gives the practical starting point for monthly affordability.
2 - Monthly outflows

How much leaves the household each month? Include the expenses and required commitments that your cash-flow method is designed to capture. The classification matters because fixed, variable, essential and discretionary spending behave differently.
3 - Cash-flow surplus or deficit
Subtract the included monthly outflows from net monthly income. If income is 8,000 and outflows are 6,200, the surplus is 1,800. A negative result is a deficit.
[VISUAL] 8,000 income - 6,200 outflows = 1,800 surplus.
4 - Savings rate

The savings rate puts that surplus in proportion to income. Using the same example, 1,800 divided by 8,000 is 22.5%. That helps compare months or households of different size. But one strong month does not automatically mean the trend is strong.
5 - Emergency-fund coverage

Ask how many months of essential expenses your eligible liquid emergency assets could cover. If liquid emergency funds are 12,000 and essential monthly expenses are 4,000, that is three months of coverage.
Do not use the total value of your home or a long-term investment as if it were immediately available emergency cash.
6 - Debt position and repayment pressure

Debt needs two views. One is the outstanding balance relative to income or assets. The other is cash-flow pressure: how much of monthly income is already committed to required repayments. FHIP keeps its Debt-to-Income and Debt Service measures separate because they answer different questions.
7 - Net worth

Net worth is assets minus liabilities at a point in time. It shows accumulated balance-sheet position, not monthly affordability. A positive net worth can coexist with weak cash flow, and a negative net worth can improve over time if debt is being reduced and assets are growing.
Put the seven numbers together

No single number wins. Income shows capacity. Outflows show demands. Surplus and savings rate show what is left. Emergency months show resilience. Debt measures show obligations. Net worth shows accumulated position.
Together, they create a much clearer financial-health picture than checking the bank balance alone.
FHIP connection and CTA
FHIP is designed to calculate and display these numbers from one canonical household data set, then connect them to the Financial Health Score, goals, forecasts and reports.
Use FHIP to check your financial health, and follow @GKTC for more practical explanations of the numbers behind household finances.

title: How to Read Your FHIP Premium Report

data.text: 30-second answer

The FHIP Premium Report is designed to read like a connected financial review rather than a collection of dashboard screenshots. Start with the report context and data confidence, then read the executive financial position, cash-flow capacity, balance sheet, liquidity and debt, wealth-building areas, goals, resilience, forecasts and the ranked action plan. Every narrative should be grounded in verified FHIP calculations and approved rules. The report may be about 16-22 pages for a standard household under the current V3 design direction, but the active production template is authoritative and the length should change when sections are not relevant.
Key takeaways

items: The Premium Report should tell one household financial story using the same canonical facts as the Dashboard, Scores and Forecasting modules.
Read the first few pages for orientation, headline strengths, concerns and actions; use later pages for evidence and detail.
Charts should answer a question and include a plain-English interpretation, not merely repeat labels.
Narratives must come from deterministic facts, rules and governed content; generative AI must not decide what is financially true.

The report is deeper than the Free Report because it can add diagnostics, history, scenarios, goals, investments, retirement, resilience, benchmark/cross-border context and a prioritised plan where those features are valid.

data.text: 1 - Confirm the report context before reading the conclusions

Begin with the household, reporting period, snapshot date, reporting currency, report version and data-confidence information. These details tell you what information the report is using and whether the analysis is current enough to support the conclusions.

A Premium Report should not hide uncertainty. Missing insurance data, stale balances, incomplete history or unavailable FX information should reduce confidence or limit specific sections rather than being silently replaced with zeros.
2 - Use the executive financial position as the map

The current V3 design direction places the household story near the front: a short executive review, headline metrics, key strengths, areas requiring attention and the highest-priority next actions. This is the map for the rest of the report.

Treat that summary as an index of what matters, not as a substitute for the evidence. If the summary says cash flow is strong but retirement readiness is weaker, later sections should show the surplus, savings rate, retirement balance, forecast assumptions and gap that support the statement.
3 - Read cash flow before judging what actions are feasible

Cash flow shows whether the household has current capacity to act. Income, expenses, required commitments, surplus/deficit and savings rate help answer whether there is room to build liquidity, reduce debt, invest or increase goal contributions.

A recommendation that ignores current capacity can be mathematically attractive but practically impossible. The Premium Report should therefore connect actions to available surplus and competing commitments rather than list isolated suggestions.
4 - Separate balance-sheet strength from short-term flexibility

The balance-sheet section explains what the household owns and owes. Net worth can be strong while liquidity is weak if most value sits in property or other less-liquid assets. Debt can be manageable in total but still create high monthly repayment pressure.
The report should therefore read net worth, liquid assets, emergency-fund coverage, debt-to-income, debt-service burden and concentration together rather than treating one metric as the whole answer.
5 - Review wealth building, retirement and protection as connected systems

Investment allocation, concentration, retirement contributions and insurance/protection address different risks. Investments may support long-term growth, retirement accounts may have restricted access, and protection can reduce the financial impact of specified events.
The Premium Report should explain these relationships without recommending a specific security, fund, insurer or product unless FHIP later operates under an approved advice framework.
6 - Read goals and forecasts as scenarios, not promises

Goal and retirement forecasts depend on current balances, contributions, time horizons and approved return/inflation assumptions. Scenario pages should show why outcomes diverge when assumptions or actions change.

Base, conservative/stress or better scenarios are planning tools. They do not predict markets. A useful report explains the assumptions and the main driver of the gap rather than presenting a smooth future line as certainty.
7 - Use the action plan as sequencing, not a shopping list

The V3 direction is to rank a small number of actions by importance and show why each matters, the evidence behind it, the gap or issue, expected direction of impact and a review timeframe. Where useful, actions can be sequenced across the next 30, 90 and 365 days.

An action should point back to a verified FHIP issue such as low emergency coverage, high repayment pressure, an unfunded goal or incomplete protection data. It should not be selected because a product is available to sell.
Worked reading example

Illustrative example: a household has a strong monthly surplus and adequate emergency liquidity, but its retirement forecast remains below the approved target pathway. The report may explain that current cash flow creates capacity, confirm that the liquidity buffer is not the immediate constraint, then identify retirement contribution modelling as a next review step. The calculation engine decides the surplus, liquidity and retirement gap; the story engine only selects the approved explanation that connects those facts.

This is the core Premium Report principle: calculation engine decides what is true; rule engine decides what matters; narrative library decides how to explain it; report composer decides where it appears.
What the Premium Report should never do

items: Recalculate a metric differently from the Dashboard or Score engine.
Invent a trend when no valid earlier snapshot exists.
Create a personalised investment or insurance product recommendation from general data.
Treat a missing value as zero merely to complete a chart.
Use generative AI to create unsupported financial facts, thresholds or benchmark claims.
Make the report longer simply because more modules exist; irrelevant sections should be omitted or replaced with a clear fallback.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
Is the Premium Report personal financial advice?
No. The design aims to feel thoughtful and connected, but it remains an educational financial-health report unless an approved regulated-advice framework is introduced.
Why can the number of pages change?
A household with no cross-border assets or no valid history should not receive empty cross-border or trend pages. The report should be dynamic.
Will AI write the Premium Report?

The current V3 direction does not require generative AI. Verified calculations, rules and governed narrative components can create the report. AI can be a future explanation layer only if safely grounded.
Why are charts accompanied by text?
A chart should explain what changed, why it matters and what to review next. Accessible table/text alternatives also make the evidence easier to verify.
How is Premium different from Free?

Premium can provide deeper diagnostics, history, forecasts, scenario comparisons, investment/retirement/goal depth, benchmark/cross-border analysis and a more developed action plan, while using the same canonical financial facts.
CTA: Open My Premium Report

title: Debt-to-Income Ratio Explained

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief

Explain FHIP’s balance-based debt-to-income measure as total included liabilities divided by gross annual household income, while warning that other lenders and jurisdictions may use different DTI definitions.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook
If a household owes 400,000 and earns 100,000 a year, is that debt high or low? The answer depends on what you are trying to measure. One useful starting point is debt-to-income.
[VISUAL] 400,000 debt / 100,000 annual income = 4.0x.
What FHIP DTI measures

FHIP’s current balance-based debt-to-income measure compares total included household liabilities with gross annual household income. Using the example, 400,000 divided by 100,000 equals 4.0 times annual income.
This is a leverage measure. It tells you how large the debt balance is relative to annual gross income. It does not tell you the monthly repayment amount.
Why definitions can differ

Here is an important warning: DTI is not defined the same way everywhere. Some lenders use monthly debt payments divided by monthly gross income. FHIP uses a balance-based measure for its household financial-health framework. Always compare formulas before comparing ratios.
Worked comparison

Household A owes 200,000 and earns 100,000: FHIP DTI is 2.0x. Household B owes 500,000 and earns 100,000: 5.0x. The second household has more leverage relative to income, but that alone does not tell us whether repayments are affordable.
[VISUAL] 2.0x vs 5.0x bars, with separate “repayment pressure?” question.
DTI is not debt service

For monthly pressure, FHIP uses a separate debt-service ratio: required monthly debt repayments divided by net monthly income. A household can have a large debt balance with a manageable current repayment, or a smaller balance with high monthly pressure.
What else matters

Interest rate, remaining loan term, whether debt is secured, income stability, liquid reserves, asset quality and repayment flexibility all add context. There is no single global household DTI threshold that can safely determine whether debt is “good” or “bad.”
FHIP connection and CTA
FHIP uses DTI as one part of the debt and financial-health picture. Review your debt position to see balances, repayments and other debt metrics together.
And follow @GKTC for more plain-English explanations of household finance.

title: Asset

data.text: Approved plain-English definition
An asset is something of economic value owned by a person or household.
What it means

Assets can include cash, bank deposits, property, investments, business interests and retirement balances, depending on the context. An asset is not automatically liquid: a home may have substantial value but cannot usually be turned into usable cash as quickly as money in a bank account.
Mini example
If a household owns a property worth 600,000 and has 20,000 in cash, both are assets. Their liquidity and role in financial planning are very different.
Related terms
Liability, Net Worth, Liquidity
FHIP contextual use

Use “Asset” consistently when FHIP explains items the household owns or controls that have economic value. Whether a record is included in a particular FHIP calculation depends on the current data dictionary and status/eligibility rules.

title: Net Worth Explained in 5 Minutes

data.text: Production status

Script and transcript draft complete. YouTube is the source of truth. Do not create a fake YouTube ID, URL, duration, thumbnail, view count or publication date. Publish on @GKTC first, then add the real metadata to the FHIP CMS record.
Production brief
Explain net worth as included assets minus included liabilities, show a simple balance-sheet example, distinguish net worth from income and liquidity, and connect to FHIP no-double-counting logic.
Target runtime: 4-8 minutes. Format: 16:9 explainer video with 2-4 supporting graphics plus complete transcript.
Full narrator script / transcript
Opening hook
If you stopped looking at salary for one minute and asked, “What do I own, and what do I owe?” you would be looking at the idea behind net worth.
[VISUAL] Two columns: Own vs Owe, merging into Net Worth.
The basic definition

Net worth is the value of your assets minus your liabilities at a point in time. Assets can include cash, property, investments and retirement balances under the relevant framework. Liabilities include amounts you owe, such as mortgages, personal loans or credit-card balances.
Worked example

Suppose a household has 20,000 of cash, a 500,000 property, 80,000 of investments and 100,000 of retirement savings. Total included assets are 700,000. If the mortgage is 350,000 and other debt is 5,000, liabilities are 355,000. Net worth is 345,000.
[VISUAL] 700,000 assets - 355,000 liabilities = 345,000 net worth.
What net worth does not tell you

Net worth does not show whether you can comfortably pay this month’s bills. A person can have a high net worth but very little accessible cash if most wealth is tied up in property. That is why liquidity, cash flow and debt repayments still matter.
Income and net worth are different

Income is money earned over a period. Net worth is an accumulated balance at one date. Income can help build net worth when some of it is saved, invested or used to reduce debt, but a high salary does not automatically create a strong balance sheet.
Avoid double counting

If an investment is also linked to a goal, it is still the same investment. If a retirement account is shown in the Retirement module and in a consolidated report, it should still be counted once. FHIP uses canonical records and relationships so labels do not create extra assets.
FHIP connection and CTA

FHIP brings included assets, investments, retirement balances and liabilities into one net-worth view while preserving categories and currencies. If you want to see the balance-sheet side of your financial health, open FHIP and see your net worth.

title: Financial Health vs Wealth: What's the Difference?

data.text: 30-second answer

Wealth describes the stock of assets and economic resources you have accumulated. Financial health describes how well your overall financial position is functioning — including cash flow, debt, liquidity, resilience and progress toward goals. Wealth can strengthen financial health, but the two are not interchangeable.
Key takeaways

items: Wealth is mainly a balance-sheet concept; financial health is a broader operating condition.
A wealthy household can be financially fragile if assets are illiquid and commitments are high.
A household with modest wealth can still have strong financial health if cash flow, debt and resilience are well managed.
Use net worth to understand accumulated position and financial-health measures to understand sustainability and flexibility.

data.text: What do we mean by wealth?

In personal finance, wealth usually refers to the assets a person or household owns after considering liabilities — often expressed through net worth. Property, cash, investments, retirement assets and business interests may contribute to wealth, while mortgages and other debts reduce net worth.

Wealth matters because it can provide long-term security, options and the ability to fund future needs. But it does not automatically show whether the household can comfortably meet next month’s expenses or absorb an unexpected shock.
What do we mean by financial health?

Financial health looks at the way the financial system of the household is functioning. Can regular income support regular commitments? Is there enough liquidity for unexpected costs? Is debt manageable? Are assets growing in a way that supports future goals? Is the household exposed to one large risk?

This broader idea is closely related to established concepts of financial well-being and resilience, which focus not just on accumulated assets but also on control, shock absorption, goal progress and choice.
Why the difference matters

Consider a household that owns a valuable property but has a large mortgage, limited cash savings and very high monthly commitments. Its net worth may be substantial, yet a short interruption to income could create immediate stress.

Now consider another household with lower net worth but no high-cost debt, a stable monthly surplus and a well-funded emergency reserve. It may have less wealth today but greater short-term resilience. Neither example is automatically better in every respect; they simply show why wealth and financial health answer different questions.
Financial health can improve before wealth becomes large

Many meaningful improvements in financial health happen before a household accumulates significant wealth. Creating a sustainable monthly surplus, building the first emergency reserve, paying down expensive debt, obtaining appropriate protection and setting up consistent contributions toward goals can all strengthen the position even if total net worth changes only gradually.

This is important because people can otherwise feel that financial progress only counts when they become wealthy. In reality, increased control and resilience are valuable improvements in their own right.
Wealth can also hide concentration and liquidity risk

A high net worth can be concentrated in one property, one business or one investment. That may create exposure that is invisible if you look only at the headline total. Similarly, some assets cannot be accessed quickly or without cost.

A financial-health view therefore asks about the composition of wealth as well as the total: how much is liquid, how diversified is it, what debts sit against it, and what ongoing cash flow is required to maintain the position?
How FHIP presents the distinction

FHIP can show net worth as one core measure while separately assessing cash flow, debt, resilience, goals, investments and other components. This avoids treating a large asset balance as proof that every part of the household position is strong.

When using the platform, read the headline numbers together. A strong net-worth trend is useful, but the reasons behind that trend — and the liquidity, debt and cash-flow position supporting it — matter too.
Frequently asked questions
Is net worth the best measure of wealth?
It is one of the most common summary measures because it deducts liabilities from assets, but it still does not describe liquidity, income stability or how concentrated the assets are.
Can financial health be strong with negative net worth?

It is possible for some dimensions to be improving even when net worth remains negative — for example, a household may have positive cash flow and be consistently reducing debt. The negative net worth still matters, but it is not the only information worth tracking.
Does becoming wealthier always improve financial health?
Not automatically. Wealth can improve resilience and choice, but borrowing heavily, concentrating assets or allowing commitments to rise too quickly can weaken other parts of financial health.
